#### Hour 1 (2-3 PM): C++ Golden Reference Model
**File:** `tests/cpp/golden_model.cpp` (~500 lines)

**What you're building:**
- Bit-accurate reference model for all RTL modules
- Used to automatically check RTL correctness
- The "ground truth" for verification

**Core architecture (bullet points):**
- `class GoldenModel`:
  - Simulates entire memory subsystem in software
  - Matches RTL interface exactly (same inputs → same outputs)
  - Runs in lockstep with RTL simulation

- `struct GoldenState`:
  - `std::vector<uint8_t> memory` (entire memory space)
  - `std::array<CacheLine, 64> cache` (cache state)
  - `DMAState dma` (DMA controller state)
  - `uint64_t cycle` (current simulation cycle)

**DMA golden model methods:**
- `void dma_start(uint32_t src, uint32_t dst, size_t len)`:
  - Record transfer parameters
  - Set state to ACTIVE
- `void dma_step()`:
  - Execute one cycle of DMA state machine
  - For each word: read from memory[src], write to memory[dst]
  - Update pointers, decrement remaining
- `bool dma_done()`: Return true when transfer complete
- `std::vector<uint8_t> get_expected_memory()`: Return memory state for comparison

**Cache golden model methods:**
- `CacheResult cache_access(uint32_t addr, bool is_write, uint8_t data)`:
  - Simulate cache lookup (same algorithm as RTL)
  - Return: hit/miss, data (for reads), new cache state
- `void cache_evict(size_t index)`:
  - If dirty: write back to memory
  - Clear valid bit

**Comparison interface:**
- `bool compare_with_rtl(const RTLState& rtl_state)`:
  - Compare memory contents byte-by-byte
  - Compare cache tags and valid bits
  - Return false if any mismatch
- `std::string get_mismatch_details()`:
  - On mismatch, return detailed error message
  - Include: address, expected value, actual value, cycle

  - Read line by line (traces can be GB-sized!)
  - Extract: instruction_pointer, memory_address, access_type (R/W)
  - Use generator pattern for memory efficiency
  - Yield: `MemoryAccess(ip, addr, type, cycle)`

**Locality analysis:**
- `def analyze_temporal_locality(self, trace)`:
  - Calculate reuse distance histogram
  - Reuse distance = # unique addresses between repeat accesses
  - Low reuse distance = high temporal locality = cache-friendly
  - Return: histogram, mean, median reuse distance

- `def analyze_spatial_locality(self, trace)`:
  - Calculate stride patterns
  - Detect cache line utilization (bytes used per line fetched)
  - Low utilization = spatial prefetching less effective
  - Return: stride histogram, avg line utilization

- `def calculate_working_set(self, trace, window_size)`:
  - Sliding window analysis
  - WSS = unique addresses in window
  - Plot WSS over time (phase behavior)
  - Return: WSS timeline, min, max, avg

**Summary generation:**
- `def generate_workload_summary(self, benchmark_name)`:
  - Parse trace, run all analyses
  - Create summary dict with all metrics
  - Save to `results/workload_summaries/{benchmark}.json`
  - Print human-readable summary

  - Returns: edge list as (src, dst) pairs

**BFS trace generation:**

    - Frontier array read/write

    - Visited array updates
  - Return: list of MemoryAccess objects

- `def generate_pagerank_trace(self, iterations=10)`:
  - Simulate PageRank iterations
  - Access patterns: scatter (write), gather (read)
  - More regular than BFS but still graph-based
  - Return: trace for pagerank workload

**Characteristics:**

  - Calculate: pointer chasing depth
  - Calculate: cache line utilization (typically low!)
  - Calculate: memory-level parallelism potential

### DAY 15 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Set-Associativity Deep Dive
- **📖 Read:** Hennessy & Patterson Ch 2.2-2.3 pages 85-105 (associativity)
- **📖 Read:** Jacob/Ng/Wang Ch 3.2 pages 120-145 (set-associative caches)
- **🎥 Watch:** Onur Mutlu Lecture 4 (60:00-90:00) - Associativity trade-offs
- **📄 Paper:** "An Analytical Model for Cache Replacement" by Qureshi & Patt (2007) - optimal 
replacement
- **📄 Paper:** "Multi-Level Cache Hierarchy" - understanding L1/L2 interaction
- **Problem with direct-mapped:** Conflict misses
  - Addresses 0x1000 and 0x5000 both map to index 0
  - They THRASH: evict each other repeatedly
  - 0% hit rate even with plenty of capacity!
- **Solution: N-way set-associative**
  - 2-way: Each index has 2 slots, check both
  - 4-way: Each index has 4 slots, check all 4
- **Math for 2-way 16KB cache:**
  - 16 KB / 2 ways / 64-byte blocks = 128 sets
  - Index bits: log₂(128) = 7 bits
  - Offset bits: log₂(64) = 6 bits
  - Tag bits: 32 - 7 - 6 = 19 bits
- **Trade-off:** More ways = fewer conflicts, but more comparators
- **Write in notebook:** Set-associative address decode example

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): L2 Cache Model (C++)
**File:** `tests/cpp/l2_cache_model.cpp` (~400 lines)

**Set-associative structure:**
- `template<size_t WAYS> struct CacheSet`:
  - `std::array<CacheLine, WAYS> ways` - one line per way
  - `std::array<uint8_t, WAYS> lru_order` - track LRU ordering

- `class SetAssociativeCache`:
  - Template: `<CACHE_SIZE, LINE_SIZE, WAYS>`
  - Calculate NUM_SETS at compile time
  - `std::array<CacheSet<WAYS>, NUM_SETS> sets`

**LRU implementation:**
- `void update_lru(size_t set_idx, size_t accessed_way)`:
  - Find current position of accessed_way in lru_order
  - Shift all ways with lower positions up by 1
  - Set accessed_way to position 0 (most recently used)

- `size_t get_lru_victim(size_t set_idx)`:
  - Return way at position WAYS-1 (least recently used)

**Access method:**
- `CacheResult access(uint32_t addr, bool is_write)`:
  - Calculate set_idx and tag from address
  - Check all WAYS for hit (tag match && valid)
  - If hit: update_lru, return HIT
  - If miss: find victim, writeback if dirty, install, update_lru

**File:** `tests/cpp/cache_hierarchy.cpp` (~300 lines)

**Two-level cache hierarchy:**
- `class CacheHierarchy`:
  - `L1Cache l1_cache_` - direct-mapped 4KB
  - `L2Cache l2_cache_` - 2-way 16KB
  - `MemoryController* memory_` - for L2 misses

- `HierarchyResult access(uint32_t addr, bool is_write)`:
  - Try L1 first
  - On L1 miss: try L2
  - On L2 miss: go to memory, fill both L1 and L2
  - Return latency and hit level

- `void calculate_amat()`:
  - AMAT = L1_time + L1_miss_rate × (L2_time + L2_miss_rate × Mem_time)

### DAY 16 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): LRU Replacement Policy
- **📖 Read:** Jacob/Ng/Wang Ch 4 pages 181-220 (replacement policies)
- **📄 Paper:** "High Performance Cache Replacement Using Re-Reference Prediction" by Jaleel et al. (2010)
- **🎥 Watch:** Onur Mutlu Lecture 5 (60:00-90:00) - Replacement policies
- **LRU = Least Recently Used:** Evict the line used longest ago
- **For 2-way:** Just 1 bit per set
  - Bit = 0: Way 0 was used more recently
  - Bit = 1: Way 1 was used more recently
  - On miss: Evict the way indicated by the bit
  - On hit: Update bit to point to OTHER way
- **For 4-way:** Need 3 bits (tree-based pseudo-LRU)
- **Why LRU works:** Temporal locality - recent = likely future
- **Write in notebook:** LRU update algorithm pseudocode

- **MESI states:**
  - **M (Modified):** Only copy, dirty (memory stale)
  - **E (Exclusive):** Only copy, clean (matches memory)
  - **S (Shared):** Multiple copies exist, all clean
  - **I (Invalid):** Line is not valid
- **Write in notebook:** MESI state diagram with all transitions

#### Hour 2 (3-4 PM): DRAMSim3 Integration
**File:** `dramsim_integration/dramsim_wrapper.cpp` (~400 lines)

**What you're building:**
- Wrapper around industry-standard DRAMSim3 simulator
- Cross-validates your RTL timing against proven model
- Critical for credibility in interviews

**Setup steps (bullet points):**
- Clone: `git clone https://github.com/umd-memsys/DRAMSim3`
- Build: `cmake -B build && cmake --build build`
- Configuration: Use `configs/DDR3_1Gb_x8_1600.ini` as template

**Wrapper class:**
- `class DRAMSim3Wrapper`:
  - `dramsim3::MemorySystem* dramsim`
  - `uint64_t current_cycle`
  - `std::map<uint64_t, RequestInfo> pending_requests`

- `void initialize(const std::string& config_file)`:
  - Create DRAMSim3 memory system
  - Register callbacks for read/write completion
  - Set up logging

- `void add_request(bool is_write, uint64_t addr, uint64_t cycle)`:
  - Convert address to DRAMSim format
  - Queue request
  - Track in pending_requests

- `void run_cycles(int n)`:
  - Advance DRAMSim3 by n cycles
  - Process any completed requests
  - Update statistics

**Callback handling:**
- `void read_complete_callback(uint64_t addr)`:
  - Find in pending_requests
  - Record completion cycle
  - Calculate latency: completion - issue

- `void write_complete_callback(uint64_t addr)`:
  - Similar to read callback
  - Track write latency separately

**Comparison interface:**
- `void compare_with_rtl(std::vector<RequestResult>& rtl_results)`:
  - For each request, compare DRAMSim latency vs RTL latency
  - Flag mismatches > 5 cycles
  - Report: "RTL latency matches DRAMSim3 within X%"

#### Hour 3 (4-5 PM): Python Trace Converter
**File:** `scripts/dramsim_trace_converter.py` (~300 lines)

**What you're building:**
- Converts your RTL simulation output to DRAMSim3 format
- Enables apples-to-apples comparison
- Bridges your tools with industry standard

**Trace formats (bullet points):**
- **RTL output format** (from Verilator/VCS):
  - `<cycle> <R/W> <address>`
  - Example: `1000 R 0x00400000`

- **DRAMSim3 format** (.trc):
  - `<address> <R/W>`
  - Address is hex, no cycle info (DRAMSim handles timing)

**Converter class:**
- `class TraceConverter`:
  - `def load_rtl_trace(self, filename)`:
    - Parse RTL log format
    - Extract: cycle, type, address
    - Return list of MemoryOp objects

  - `def convert_to_dramsim(self, ops, output_file)`:
    - Write in DRAMSim format
    - Group by arrival time (DRAMSim uses request rate)
    - Handle address alignment (64-byte cache lines)

  - `def generate_comparison_trace(self, ops, output_file)`:
    - Include both RTL timing and placeholder for DRAMSim timing
    - After DRAMSim run, merge results for comparison

**Analysis functions:**
- `def analyze_request_pattern(self, ops)`:
  - Calculate: requests per bank
  - Calculate: row buffer hit rate (estimated)
  - Calculate: average burst length
  - Return: pattern summary

- `def estimate_achievable_bandwidth(self, ops, dram_config)`:
  - Based on access pattern and timing constraints
  - Theoretical max given your access pattern
  - Compare to what RTL achieves

**Deliverable:**
- DDR3 timing checker catching all JEDEC violations (~500 lines C++)
- DRAMSim3 wrapper for cross-validation (~400 lines C++)
- Trace converter for tool interoperability (~300 lines Python)
- Confidence that your RTL matches industry-standard DRAM model

    - MCF benchmark: pointer chasing, poor locality
    - Random addresses within working set
    - Low row buffer hit rate expected

  - `def generate_lbm_pattern(self, num_accesses)`:
    - LBM benchmark: streaming access
    - Sequential addresses with occasional jumps
    - High row buffer hit rate expected

  - `def generate_gcc_pattern(self, num_accesses)`:
    - GCC benchmark: mixed access
    - Combination of sequential and random
    - Medium row buffer hit rate

  - `def generate_mix_pattern(self, num_accesses)`:
    - Interleaved patterns from multiple "threads"
    - Tests scheduler fairness
    - Challenging for FR-FCFS

- `def save_trace(self, trace, filename, format='ramulator')`:

  - DRAMSim3 format: `<addr> <R/W> <cycle>`

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): Automated Documentation Generator (C++)
**File:** `src/tools/doc_generator.cpp` (~400 lines)

**DocGenerator Class - Auto-Extract Module Information:**

`class ModuleDocGenerator`:
- **Purpose:** Parse RTL files and auto-generate markdown documentation
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::vector<ModuleInfo> modules_` - Extracted module information
  - `std::map<std::string, std::string> port_descriptions_` - Port documentation from comments
  - `std::vector<ParameterInfo> parameters_` - Module parameter list
  - `std::string output_dir_` - Documentation output directory
  - `bool include_waveforms_` - Whether to generate timing diagrams

- `void parse_rtl_file(const std::string& filepath)`:
  - Open file and read line by line
  - Use regex to match `module <name> #(` for module declarations
  - Extract parameter list between `#(` and `)` parentheses
  - Parse each `parameter TYPE NAME = VALUE` with regex
  - Extract port list between module ports `(` and `);`
  - For each port, capture direction (input/output/inout), width, name
  - Look for `//` comments on same line as ports for descriptions
  - Build `ModuleInfo` struct with name, params, ports, comments

- `void extract_state_machine(const std::string& content)`:
  - Search for `typedef enum` or `localparam` with `_STATE` suffix
  - Extract all state names into vector
  - Look for `case(state)` or `case(current_state)` blocks
  - For each case item, extract the next state assignments
  - Build state transition table: `{current_state, condition, next_state}`
  - Store in `std::vector<StateTransition> transitions_`

- `void generate_port_table(std::ostream& out, const ModuleInfo& mod)`:
  - Write markdown header: `## Port Description`
  - Create table header: `| Signal | Direction | Width | Description |`
  - Loop through ports: `for (auto& port : mod.ports)`
  - Format width as `[N:0]` or `1` for single-bit
  - Write each port as markdown table row
  - Add horizontal separator at end

- `void generate_parameter_table(std::ostream& out)`:
  - Write `## Parameters` header
  - Table columns: `| Name | Type | Default | Description |`
  - For each parameter, lookup description from comments map
  - Write formatted rows with default values
  - Add usage examples section showing typical configurations

- `void generate_fsm_diagram(std::ostream& out)`:
  - Write `## State Machine` header
  - Generate Mermaid diagram syntax: `stateDiagram-v2`
  - For each state: add node `    state StateName`
  - For each transition: add edge `    StateA --> StateB : condition`
  - Wrap in markdown code fence with `mermaid` language tag
  - This renders as visual FSM in GitHub/modern viewers

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): Code Quality Analysis Framework (C++)
**File:** `src/tools/code_analyzer.cpp` (~400 lines)

**CodeQualityAnalyzer Class - RTL Linting & Metrics:**

`class RTLCodeAnalyzer`:
- **Purpose:** Analyze RTL code for style, complexity, and common issues
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::vector<LintViolation> violations_` - Style violations found
  - `std::map<std::string, ModuleMetrics> metrics_` - Complexity metrics per module
  - `std::vector<std::string> naming_conventions_` - Expected naming patterns
  - `bool strict_mode_` - Enable all checks vs essential only
  - `std::string report_path_` - Output report location

- `void check_naming_convention(const std::string& identifier, IdentifierType type)`:
  - For signals: verify snake_case format using regex `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$`
  - For modules: verify snake_case module names
  - For parameters: verify UPPER_SNAKE_CASE `^[A-Z][A-Z0-9_]*$`
  - For state names: verify `STATE_NAME` format
  - Add violation to list if pattern doesn't match
  - Include line number and suggested fix

- `void analyze_fsm_completeness(const std::string& content)`:
  - Extract all case statements with `case(...)` regex
  - Find state variable being switched on
  - Enumerate all possible states from enum definition
  - Check each case for: default clause present, all states handled
  - Verify no unreachable states (states never transitioned to)
  - Flag incomplete case statements as potential bugs

- `void calculate_cyclomatic_complexity(const ModuleInfo& mod)`:
  - Count decision points: if, case, ternary operators
  - Count loops: for, while (unusual in synthesizable RTL)
  - Cyclomatic complexity = edges - nodes + 2*connected_components
  - For RTL: simplified as 1 + number of decision points
  - Flag modules with complexity > 20 as needing refactoring
  - Store in `ModuleMetrics` struct

- `void detect_clock_domain_issues(const std::string& content)`:
  - Find all `always @(posedge ...)` blocks
  - Extract clock signal name from each block
  - If multiple unique clocks found, module is multi-clock
  - Look for signals assigned in one clock domain, read in another
  - Flag potential CDC (Clock Domain Crossing) issues
  - Suggest synchronizer patterns if CDC detected

- `void check_reset_consistency(const std::string& content)`:
  - Find all always blocks with reset logic
  - Verify reset polarity consistent (all active-high or all active-low)
  - Check that all flip-flops in module have reset
  - Identify signals assigned in reset but not in else clause (latch inference)
  - Flag inconsistent reset usage

- `void detect_latch_inference(const std::string& content)`:
  - Find all combinational always blocks: `always @(*)`
  - For each block, extract assigned signals
  - For each if/case statement, verify signal assigned in ALL branches
  - If signal not assigned in some path = latch inference warning
  - Suggest adding else clause or default assignment

**ParameterValidator Class - Check Valid Configurations:**

`class ParameterValidator`:
- **Purpose:** Validate RTL parameters before simulation to catch impossible configs

- `void parse_parameter_constraints(const std::string& rtl_path)`:
  - Look for comments with constraint hints: `// CONSTRAINT: power_of_2`
  - Build constraint map: `{param_name -> constraint_type}`
  - Common constraints: power_of_2, range(min,max), divisible_by(n)

- `void validate_cache_parameters(const CacheParams& params)`:
  - Check cache_size is power of 2
  - Check block_size <= cache_size
  - Verify cache_size % (block_size * associativity) == 0
  - Verify address_width >= log2(cache_size) + tag_bits
  - Return error messages for any violations

- `void validate_ddr3_parameters(const DDR3Params& params)`:
  - Verify burst_length in {4, 8} for DDR3
  - Check tRCD, tRP, tRAS timing relationships
  - Verify bank_count is power of 2
  - Check data_width in {4, 8, 16} per JEDEC spec
  - Flag any impossible configurations

- `void generate_constraint_report(std::ostream& out)`:
  - List all parameters with their constraints
  - Show valid ranges for each parameter
  - Provide example valid configurations
  - Save as `docs/parameter_constraints.md`

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): Constrained Random Test Generator (C++)
**File:** `src/verification/crv_generator.cpp` (~450 lines)

**ConstrainedRandomGenerator Class - Generate Valid Stimuli:**

`class ConstrainedRandomGenerator`:
- **Purpose:** Generate constrained random test vectors for RTL verification
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::mt19937_64 rng_` - Mersenne Twister random engine
  - `uint64_t seed_` - Seed for reproducibility
  - `std::vector<Constraint> constraints_` - Active constraints
  - `std::map<std::string, Distribution> distributions_` - Custom distributions
  - `TestSequence current_sequence_` - Generated test sequence

- `void set_seed(uint64_t seed)`:
  - Store seed for reproducibility
  - Initialize RNG with seed: `rng_.seed(seed)`
  - Log seed to file for regression replay
  - Reset all derived generators

- `void add_constraint(const std::string& name, ConstraintFunc func)`:
  - Create Constraint object with name and validation function
  - Add to constraints vector
  - Constraints are functions returning bool given proposed value
  - Example: `[](uint32_t addr) { return (addr & 0x3F) == 0; }` for 64-byte alignment

- `uint32_t generate_address(const AddressConstraints& c)`:
  - Create uniform distribution over valid address range
  - Generate candidate address
  - Apply alignment mask: `addr = addr & ~(c.alignment - 1)`
  - Verify against memory region constraints
  - If address in excluded regions, regenerate
  - Return valid aligned address within bounds

- `MemoryTransaction generate_transaction()`:
  - Create transaction struct
  - Generate address with current constraints
  - Select operation type with weighted distribution:
    - 70% reads, 25% writes, 5% read-modify-write
  - Generate data payload for writes (random bytes)
  - Select burst length from {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} with weights
  - Set QoS and priority fields randomly
  - Return complete transaction

- `TestSequence generate_sequence(size_t num_transactions)`:
  - Clear current sequence
  - For each transaction index:
    - Generate transaction with current constraints
    - Insert random delays between transactions (0-10 cycles)
    - Add to sequence with timestamp
  - Apply sequence-level constraints (no back-to-back to same address)
  - Return complete test sequence

**FunctionalCoverageModel Class - Track What's Tested:**

`class FunctionalCoverageModel`:
- **Purpose:** Track coverage of functional scenarios during verification
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::map<std::string, CoverPoint> coverpoints_` - Individual cover points
  - `std::map<std::string, CrossCoverage> crosses_` - Cross-coverage bins
  - `std::vector<CoverageHit> hits_` - Coverage events log
  - `double target_coverage_` - Target coverage percentage (default 90%)

- `void define_coverpoint(const std::string& name, size_t num_bins)`:
  - Create CoverPoint with specified bins
  - Initialize all bin counts to zero
  - Add to coverpoints map
  - Example: `define_coverpoint("cache_state", 4)` for MESI states

- `void define_cross(const std::string& name, std::vector<std::string> coverpoints)`:
  - Create cross-coverage between existing coverpoints
  - Calculate total bins = product of individual coverpoint bins
  - Initialize all cross bins to zero
  - Example: `define_cross("state_x_operation", {"cache_state", "op_type"})`

- `void sample(const std::string& coverpoint, size_t bin)`:
  - Increment hit count for specified bin
  - Log hit to coverage trace if first hit for bin
  - Update coverage percentage for coverpoint
  - Check if coverpoint now fully covered

- `void sample_cross(const std::string& cross_name, std::vector<size_t> bins)`:
  - Calculate flat index from multi-dimensional bin indices
  - Increment cross bin count
  - Update cross coverage percentage

- `CoverageReport generate_report()`:
  - For each coverpoint: calculate % of bins hit
  - For each cross: calculate % of cross bins hit
  - Identify coverage holes (bins never hit)
  - Calculate overall coverage weighted average
  - Return structured report with recommendations

**DRAMSim3 Test Interface:**

`class DRAMSim3TestInterface`:
- **Purpose:** Run generated tests through DRAMSim3 for validation
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::unique_ptr<dramsim3::MemorySystem> memory_sys_` - DRAMSim3 instance
  - `std::queue<PendingRequest> pending_` - Requests awaiting completion
  - `std::vector<CompletedRequest> completed_` - Completed requests

- `void initialize(const std::string& config_file)`:
  - Create DRAMSim3 memory system with config
  - Register read and write callbacks
  - Set clock period based on DDR frequency
  - Log DRAMSim3 version for reproducibility

- `void submit_test_sequence(const TestSequence& seq)`:
  - For each transaction in sequence:
    - Wait until transaction's scheduled cycle
    - Call `memory_sys_->AddTransaction(addr, is_write)`
    - Add to pending queue with expected result
    - Tick DRAMSim3 clock

- `void verify_results(const TestSequence& expected)`:
  - Compare completed transactions against expected
  - For reads: verify data matches expected
  - For writes: verify write completion callback received
  - Report any mismatches with cycle and address
  - Calculate pass rate

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): Protocol Checker Generator (C++)
**File:** `src/verification/protocol_checker.cpp` (~400 lines)

**ProtocolCheckerGenerator Class - Auto-Generate Protocol Assertions:**

`class ProtocolCheckerGenerator`:
- **Purpose:** Auto-generate SVA assertions from protocol specifications
- **Member variables:**
  - `ProtocolSpec axi_spec_` - AXI4 protocol rules
  - `ProtocolSpec mesi_spec_` - MESI coherence rules
  - `std::vector<GeneratedAssertion> assertions_` - Output assertions
  - `std::string output_path_` - Generated SVA file path
  - `bool formal_mode_` - Generate for formal verification

- `void load_axi4_specification()`:
  - Define AXI handshake rules:
    - VALID must stay high until READY acknowledged
    - VALID cannot depend on READY
    - WLAST must be asserted on final beat
  - Define ordering rules:
    - Write responses must match request order per AW ID
    - Read data must be in order for same AR ID
  - Store as structured `ProtocolRule` objects with SVA templates

- `void load_mesi_specification()`:
  - Define exclusive states:
    - Only one cache can be in Modified for same line
    - Only one cache can be in Exclusive for same line
  - Define transition rules:
    - M→S requires writeback before downgrade
    - I→M requires invalidation broadcast
  - Define coherence invariants:
    - If any cache is M, memory is stale
    - If any cache is E or M, no other cache is valid

- `void generate_axi_assertions(const std::string& interface_name)`:
  - For each AXI rule in specification:
    - Substitute interface name into SVA template
    - Generate immediate assertion for combinational checks
    - Generate concurrent assertion for temporal checks
  - Create assertion for AWVALID stability:
    - `property awvalid_stable; @(posedge clk) (awvalid && !awready) |=> awvalid; endproperty`
  - Create assertion for burst count:
    - Track beats, verify WLAST on final beat
  - Output to `{interface_name}_axi_checker.sv`

- `void generate_mesi_assertions(const std::string& coherence_module)`:
  - Generate invariant checks for each cache line:
    - `assert property (@(posedge clk) !(core0_state==M && core1_state==M))`
  - Generate transition legality checks:
    - Build state machine of legal transitions
    - Check `(prev_state, curr_state)` is legal transition
  - Generate memory consistency checks:
    - If cache is M, verify memory has old value
    - After writeback, verify memory updated

**AssertionCompiler Class - Compile to DRAMSim3/Ramulator Monitors:**

`class AssertionCompiler`:
- **Purpose:** Convert assertions to C++ runtime monitors for tool validation
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::vector<ParsedAssertion> parsed_` - Parsed assertion ASTs
  - `std::map<std::string, SignalID> signal_map_` - Signal name to ID mapping
  - `std::string cpp_output_path_` - Output C++ monitor file

- `void parse_sva_file(const std::string& sva_path)`:
  - Read SVA file line by line
  - Use regex to extract `property` definitions
  - Parse sequence operators: `|->`, `|=>`, `##`, `[*]`
  - Build AST representation of each property
  - Store in parsed assertions vector

- `void compile_to_cpp_monitor()`:
  - For each parsed assertion:
    - Generate C++ class with `sample()` method
    - Translate temporal operators to state machines:
      - `|->` (implication): if antecedent matches, check consequent
      - `##1`: check consequent on next cycle
      - `[*N]`: check for N consecutive cycles
    - Generate error reporting on assertion failure

- `void generate_dramsim3_hooks(std::ostream& out)`:
  - Create callback functions for DRAMSim3 events
  - Hook transaction completion to sample assertions
  - Hook command issuance for timing assertions
  - Generate registration code for DRAMSim3 callback system

      - Protocol (AXI, AHB, etc.) - contains interface keywords
      - FSM (state machine) - references state variables
      - Timing (clock cycles) - uses `##` operator
      - Invariant (always true) - no temporal operators
    - Count assertions per category
  
  - `def check_module_coverage(self)`:
    - List all RTL modules in project
    - For each module, count assertions
    - Flag modules with < 3 assertions as "under-covered"
    - Calculate assertion density (assertions per 100 lines)
    - Return report with recommendations

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): Performance Profiler Framework (C++)
**File:** `src/profiling/performance_profiler.cpp` (~450 lines)

**PerformanceProfiler Class - Cycle-Accurate Analysis:**

`class PerformanceProfiler`:
- **Purpose:** Track cycle-by-cycle performance of memory subsystem
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::map<std::string, ComponentProfile> component_profiles_` - Per-component stats
  - `std::vector<StallEvent> stall_events_` - Detailed stall log
  - `uint64_t total_cycles_` - Total simulation cycles
  - `uint64_t active_cycles_` - Cycles doing useful work
  - `BottleneckAnalysis bottleneck_` - Identified bottlenecks

- `void register_component(const std::string& name, ComponentType type)`:
  - Create ComponentProfile entry
  - Initialize cycle counters to zero
  - Set component type (CACHE, MEMORY, DMA, COHERENCE)
  - Add state tracking (IDLE, ACTIVE, STALLED, WAITING)
  - Register with profiler's component list

- `void record_state_change(const std::string& component, State new_state, uint64_t cycle)`:
  - Look up component profile
  - Calculate duration in previous state: `cycle - last_transition_cycle_`
  - Increment counter for previous state by duration
  - If new state is STALLED:
    - Record stall start cycle
    - Note stall cause if available
  - Update last_transition_cycle_ to current cycle
  - Update current_state_

- `void record_memory_access(const MemoryAccess& access)`:
  - Log access with timestamp, address, type
  - Track latency from request to completion
  - Categorize as L1_HIT, L2_HIT, DRAM_ACCESS
  - Update hit rate counters for each cache level
  - For DRAM access: track which timing constraint delayed it

- `void record_stall_event(const StallEvent& event)`:
  - Store full stall event with:
    - Component causing stall
    - Component waiting
    - Duration in cycles
    - Cause (full_queue, bank_conflict, coherence_wait, etc.)
  - Update stall statistics by cause
  - Update stall statistics by component

- `BottleneckAnalysis identify_bottlenecks()`:
  - Calculate stall percentage per component: `stall_cycles / total_cycles`
  - Rank components by stall contribution
  - For each top staller, identify primary cause
  - Calculate theoretical speedup if bottleneck removed (Amdahl's Law)
  - Return ranked list with improvement potential

**WorkloadGenerator Class - Benchmark Patterns:**

`class WorkloadGenerator`:
- **Purpose:** Generate realistic memory access patterns for profiling
- **Member variables:**
  - `WorkloadType current_type_` - Current benchmark type
  - `uint64_t num_accesses_` - Total accesses to generate
  - `std::vector<MemoryRequest> requests_` - Generated request stream

- `void generate_sequential_scan(uint64_t start_addr, uint64_t size)`:
  - Create accesses from start_addr to start_addr + size
  - Stride by cache line size (64 bytes)
  - All reads, no writes
  - Expected: Very high cache hit rate after warmup
  - Log expected hit rate based on cache size

- `void generate_random_accesses(uint64_t addr_range, size_t count)`:
  - Use uniform distribution over address range
  - Randomly select read (80%) or write (20%)
  - No address alignment (stress cache)
  - Expected: Low hit rate, high memory traffic

- `void generate_strided_pattern(uint64_t start, uint64_t stride, size_t count)`:
  - Matrix access pattern: A[i][j] with column-major stride
  - Stride typically = row_size (conflict misses)
  - Useful for measuring cache associativity effects
  - Log expected conflict miss rate

- `void generate_producer_consumer(size_t buffer_size, size_t iterations)`:
  - Simulate two cores sharing a circular buffer
  - Producer writes to head, consumer reads from tail
  - Creates coherence traffic (MESI transitions)
  - Stress test for coherence protocol

- `void generate_mixed_workload(const MixRatios& ratios)`:
  - Combine multiple patterns with specified ratios
  - e.g., 50% sequential, 30% random, 20% strided
  - More realistic than single-pattern benchmarks

**DRAMSim3 Profiling Integration:**

`class DRAMSim3Profiler`:
- **Purpose:** Extract detailed profiling from DRAMSim3 simulation
- **Member variables:**
  - `dramsim3::MemorySystem* memory_sys_` - DRAMSim3 instance
  - `std::vector<ChannelStats> channel_stats_` - Per-channel statistics
  - `std::vector<BankStats> bank_stats_` - Per-bank statistics

- `void capture_statistics()`:
  - Query DRAMSim3 for internal statistics
  - Extract per-bank utilization
  - Extract queue depths over time
  - Extract timing constraint hit counts (tRCD, tRP, tRAS, tRRD)
  - Store in structured stats objects

- `void calculate_row_buffer_efficiency()`:
  - Count row hits vs row misses per bank
  - Row buffer hit rate = row_hits / (row_hits + row_misses)
  - Compare to theoretical maximum for workload
  - Identify if scheduling can improve

- `void compare_scheduling_policies(const std::vector<std::string>& policies)`:
  - For each scheduling policy (FCFS, FR-FCFS, PAR-BS):
    - Run same workload through DRAMSim3
    - Collect bandwidth and latency statistics
  - Create comparison table
  - Identify best policy for workload type

**OptimizationTracker Class - Track and Compare Optimizations:**

`class OptimizationTracker`:

  - `std::vector<OptimizationRun> optimized_runs_` - Post-optimization results

- `void run_optimization_comparison(const std::string& optimization_name)`:
  - Run same 5 benchmarks with optimization enabled
  - Collect same metrics as baseline
  - Calculate delta for each metric
  - Calculate percentage improvement
  - Flag any regressions (metric got worse)
  - Store results in optimized_runs_

- `Improvement calculate_improvement(const std::string& metric)`:
  - Find baseline value for metric
  - Find optimized value for metric
  - Calculate absolute improvement: `optimized - baseline`
  - Calculate percentage improvement: `(optimized - baseline) / baseline * 100`
  - Determine if statistically significant (run 5 times, check variance)
  - Return Improvement struct

- `void apply_amdahls_law_projection(const BottleneckList& bottlenecks)`:
  - For each bottleneck, get fraction of execution time
  - Calculate theoretical speedup if completely fixed
  - Calculate speedup for partial fixes (50%, 75%, 100%)
  - Create priority ranking by `speedup * ease_of_fix`
  - Store projections for comparison with actual results

### Hour 1-2 (9:30-11:30 AM): Automated Gate Check Runner (C++)
**File:** `src/gate_check/gate_check_runner.cpp` (~450 lines)

**GateCheckRunner Class - Automated Verification Pipeline:**

`class GateCheckRunner`:
- **Purpose:** Run all gate check tests automatically with pass/fail determination
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::vector<GateCheckTest> tests_` - All gate check tests
  - `std::map<std::string, Requirement> requirements_` - Pass/fail criteria
  - `std::vector<TestResult> results_` - Test outcomes
  - `std::string report_path_` - Report output location
  - `DRAMSim3Interface* dramsim3_` - Industry tool validator

- `void define_month1_requirements()`:
  - Add DMA requirement: `{"dma_bandwidth", ">=", 500, "MB/s"}`
  - Add L1 cache requirement: `{"l1_hit_rate", ">=", 85, "%"}`
  - Add L2 cache requirement: `{"l2_hit_rate", ">=", 95, "%"}`
  - Add DDR3 requirement: `{"ddr3_bandwidth", ">=", 600, "MB/s"}`
  - Add test count requirement: `{"test_count", ">=", 2000, "tests"}`
  - Add coverage requirement: `{"coverage", ">=", 90, "%"}`
  - Add coherence requirement: `{"mesi_assertions", "==", 0, "failures"}`

- `TestResult run_dma_gate_check()`:
  - Initialize DMA benchmark harness
  - Run sequential transfer test (64KB blocks, 1000 iterations)
  - Run burst mode test (variable burst 4-16 beats)
  - Run random address test (addresses across 4GB space)
  - Collect bandwidth measurements for each pattern
  - Calculate average bandwidth: `total_bytes / total_cycles * clock_freq`
  - Compare against 500 MB/s threshold
  - Return TestResult with measured value and pass/fail

- `TestResult run_cache_gate_check()`:
  - Initialize cache benchmark harness
  - Run sequential scan across 1MB (expect near 100% L1 hit after warmup)
  - Run working set sweep: 2KB, 4KB, 8KB, 16KB, 32KB
  - Measure hit rate at each working set size
  - Verify L1 hit rate >= 85% for appropriate working sets
  - Verify L2 hit rate >= 95% for L1 misses
  - Test LRU replacement correctness with directed test
  - Return TestResult for each cache level

- `TestResult run_coherence_gate_check()`:
  - Initialize MESI protocol test harness
  - Run producer-consumer test:
    - Core 0 writes to shared buffer
    - Core 1 reads from shared buffer
    - Verify data consistency across 1000 iterations
  - Run random shared access test:
    - Both cores randomly read/write shared region
    - Check all assertions pass
  - Run ping-pong stress test:
    - Cores alternate writing to same cache line
    - Verify MESI transitions are correct
  - Count assertion failures
  - Return TestResult with failure count

- `TestResult run_ddr3_gate_check()`:
  - Initialize DDR3 benchmark harness
  - Run sequential bandwidth test
  - Measure row buffer hit rate
  - Compare FR-FCFS vs FCFS scheduling:
    - Run same workload with each scheduler
    - Calculate bandwidth improvement
  - Validate against DRAMSim3:
    - Run identical workload in DRAMSim3
    - Compare bandwidth within 5% tolerance
  - Return TestResult with bandwidth and validation status

- `void run_all_gate_checks()`:
  - Execute each gate check in sequence
  - Store results in results_ vector
  - Calculate overall pass count
  - Determine gate check overall status
  - Generate summary report

**DRAMSim3ValidationRunner Class:**

`class DRAMSim3ValidationRunner`:
- **Purpose:** Validate RTL results against DRAMSim3 industry tool
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::unique_ptr<dramsim3::MemorySystem> dramsim3_` - DRAMSim3 instance
  - `std::vector<ValidationResult> validations_` - Validation results

- `void configure_matching_parameters()`:
  - Set DRAMSim3 timing to match RTL:
    - tRCD, tRP, tRAS, tCAS from RTL parameters
    - DDR3-1600 timing profile
    - Same number of banks, ranks, channels
  - Verify configuration loaded correctly

- `ValidationResult compare_bandwidth(const Workload& workload)`:
  - Run workload through RTL simulation, measure bandwidth
  - Run same workload through DRAMSim3, measure bandwidth
  - Calculate percentage difference
  - Pass if difference < 5%
  - Log detailed comparison for debugging

- `ValidationResult compare_latency_distribution(const Workload& workload)`:
  - Run workload through RTL, collect latency histogram
  - Run same workload through DRAMSim3, collect histogram
  - Compare histogram shapes using statistical test
  - Pass if distributions statistically similar
  - Flag outliers for investigation

**VerificationAnalyzer Class - Comprehensive Verification Metrics:**

`class VerificationAnalyzer`:
- **Purpose:** Aggregate and analyze all verification metrics for gate check
- **Member variables:**
  - `std::vector<TestSuite> test_suites_` - All test suites with results
  - `CoverageData coverage_` - Code and functional coverage
  - `std::vector<Assertion> assertions_` - All assertions with hit counts
  - `uint64_t total_tests_` - Total test count
  - `uint64_t passing_tests_` - Passing test count

- `void load_test_results(const std::string& results_dir)`:
  - Scan results directory for test output files
  - Parse each test result: name, status (pass/fail), duration, output
  - Categorize by suite: unit, integration, random, directed
  - Calculate pass rate per suite
  - Aggregate total test count

- `void load_coverage_data(const std::string& coverage_dir)`:
  - Parse Verilator coverage.dat file
  - Extract line coverage per module
  - Extract branch coverage for conditionals
  - Extract FSM state coverage
  - Load functional coverage from JSON
  - Calculate overall coverage percentages

- `TestResult verify_test_count_requirement()`:
  - Count total passing tests
  - Compare against 2000 minimum requirement
  - Calculate margin (how many above/below threshold)
  - Return TestResult with pass/fail status
  - If failing, identify which suites need more tests

- `TestResult verify_coverage_requirement()`:
  - Calculate weighted coverage:
    - Line coverage: 40% weight
    - Branch coverage: 30% weight
    - FSM coverage: 20% weight
    - Functional coverage: 10% weight
  - Compare against 90% minimum
  - If failing, identify lowest-covered modules
  - Return TestResult with coverage breakdown

- `void identify_coverage_holes()`:
  - Find all lines with 0 hits
  - Find all branches with 0 hits
  - Find all FSM states never reached
  - Find all coverpoints with 0 hits
  - Prioritize by importance (FSM > functional > branch > line)
  - Generate list of recommended tests to add

- `void generate_verification_report(std::ostream& out)`:
  - Create comprehensive verification status report
  - Include test count by category
  - Include coverage breakdown by module
  - Include assertion summary
  - List any coverage holes with suggestions
  - Calculate overall verification confidence score

**SynthesisAnalyzer Class - Parse Synthesis Results:**

`class SynthesisAnalyzer`:
- **Purpose:** Parse Vivado synthesis reports and verify timing/resources
- **Member variables:**
  - `TimingReport timing_` - WNS, TNS, failing paths
  - `ResourceReport resources_` - LUTs, FFs, BRAMs, DSPs
  - `std::vector<SynthesisWarning> warnings_` - All warnings

- `void parse_timing_report(const std::string& report_path)`:
  - Open Vivado timing_summary.rpt
  - Search for "Worst Negative Slack" line
  - Extract WNS value in ns
  - Search for "Total Negative Slack" line
  - Extract TNS value
  - If WNS < 0, extract failing path endpoints
  - Store in timing_ struct

- `void parse_resource_report(const std::string& report_path)`:
  - Open Vivado utilization.rpt
  - Extract LUT count and percentage
  - Extract FF count and percentage
  - Extract BRAM count and percentage
  - Extract DSP count and percentage
  - Flag if any resource > 80% as "tight"

- `TestResult verify_timing_requirement()`:
  - Check WNS >= 0 (timing met)
  - Check TNS == 0 (no accumulated violations)
  - If passing with margin > 1ns, suggest increasing clock
  - If failing, identify critical paths for optimization
  - Return TestResult with timing status

- `void parse_synthesis_warnings(const std::string& log_path)`:
  - Scan Vivado synthesis log for "WARNING:"
  - Categorize warnings:
    - Latch inference (critical)
    - Unused signals (minor)
    - Width mismatches (important)
    - Black box instantiation (check)
  - Flag any critical warnings for review
  - Count warnings by severity

**Ramulator Integration for DDR Validation:**

`class RamulatorValidator`:
- **Purpose:** Cross-validate memory controller against Ramulator
- **Member variables:**
  - `ramulator::Memory* ramulator_` - Ramulator instance
  - `std::vector<ComparisonResult> comparisons_` - Validation results

- `void configure_ramulator(const DDRConfig& config)`:
  - Set memory type to DDR3
  - Configure timing: tRCD, tRP, tRAS, tCAS
  - Set organization: banks, ranks, channels
  - Set address mapping scheme
  - Enable statistics collection

- `ComparisonResult validate_scheduling(const Workload& workload)`:
  - Run workload through RTL memory controller
  - Run same workload through Ramulator
  - Compare command sequences:
    - Are ACT, PRE, READ, WRITE in same order?
    - Are bank accesses interleaved similarly?
  - Calculate scheduling similarity score
  - Return comparison with detailed diff

### 📚 DAY 32 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Snooping Scalability Limits

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** Hennessy & Patterson Ch 5.4-5.5 pages 400-420 (coherence scalability)
- **📖 Read:** "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence" Ch 6-7 (directory protocols)
  - **Free PDF:** Search "Synthesis Lectures Memory Consistency Primer"

**Video (1 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** Onur Mutlu Lecture 13 "Directory-Based Coherence" (first half, 45m)
- **🎥 Watch:** Hot Chips presentation on AMD Infinity Fabric scalability (15m)

**Key Concepts:**
- **The bus bandwidth problem:**
  - Snooping: EVERY cache watches EVERY transaction
  - N cores → N snoop checks per transaction
  - Bus becomes bottleneck at ~4-8 cores
- **Quantitative analysis:**
  - Bus bandwidth: 10 GB/s typical
  - Each core: 2 GB/s demand
  - Snoops add 50% overhead
  - Math: 4 cores × 2 GB/s × 1.5 = 12 GB/s > 10 GB/s = BOTTLENECK
- **Architect insight:** This is why AMD/Intel use mesh networks, not buses
- **Write in notebook:** Scalability graph (cores vs. effective bandwidth)

### 📚 DAY 33 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): How Directories Work

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence" Ch 8-9 (directory protocols)
- **📖 Read:** Hennessy & Patterson Ch 5.5 pages 420-440

**Video + Paper (1 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** Onur Mutlu Lecture 13 (continued from Day 32, 45:00-end)
- **📄 Paper:** "SGI Origin: A CCNUMA Server" - Real directory implementation

**Key Concepts:**
- **Directory = centralized tracking:**
  - For each cache line, track: Which caches have a copy?
  - States: Uncached, Shared, Exclusive/Modified
  - Sharer vector: 1 bit per core
- **Directory operations:**
  - READ: Check directory, forward to sharers if needed
  - WRITE: Check directory, invalidate all sharers
  - WRITEBACK: Update directory, clear sharer
- **Why this scales:**
  - NO broadcast! Only contact known sharers
  - 16 sharers vs. 16 broadcasts = massive savings
- **Write in notebook:** Directory state machine diagram

### 📚 DAY 34 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Directory Protocol Messages

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence" Ch 9 pages 120-150
- **🌐 Website:** https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~418/lectures/ - CMU 15-418 lecture slides on coherence

**Key Concepts:**
- **Request messages (core → directory):**
  - GetS: Read request (get Shared copy)
  - GetM: Write request (get Modified, need exclusive)
  - PutS/PutM: Writeback (release line)
- **Response messages (directory → core):**
  - Data: Here's the data you requested
  - Inv-Ack: Acknowledgment of invalidation
- **Forward messages (directory → sharer):**
  - Fwd-GetS: Forward read request to owner
  - Inv: Invalidate your copy
- **Write in notebook:** Full message flow for read-then-write

### 📚 DAY 36 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): The False Sharing Problem

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📄 Paper:** Drepper "What Every Programmer..." Section 3.4.1 (pages 47-50) - False sharing
- **📄 Paper:** "Eliminating False Sharing" by Eggers & Jeremiassen (1991)

**Video (0.5 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** "False Sharing Explained" on YouTube (any C++ performance channel, 15 min)

**Key Concepts:**
- **Definition:** Two cores access DIFFERENT data in SAME cache line
  - Core A writes word 0 of line X
  - Core B writes word 1 of line X
  - They don't share data, but they share the LINE
  - Line bounces back and forth = "ping-pong"
- **Performance impact:**
  - Can be 10-100× slowdown!
  - Common in parallel programs
  - Often hidden (not obvious from code)
- **Detection:**
  - Count invalidations per line
  - High invalidation + different word accesses = false sharing

### 📚 DAY 37 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): What is Memory Consistency?

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** "A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence" Ch 3-5 (THE definitive treatment)
- **📄 Paper:** "Shared Memory Consistency Models: A Tutorial" by Adve & Gharachorloo (1996)
  - **Classic paper - read the whole thing (30 pages)**

**Video (0.5 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** Onur Mutlu Lecture 14 "Memory Consistency" (first 30 min)

**Key Concepts:**
- **Coherence vs. Consistency:**
  - Coherence: All see same value for same location (solved with MESI)
  - Consistency: In what ORDER do writes become visible?
- **Sequential Consistency (SC):**
  - All operations appear in some total order
  - Simplest to program, but SLOWEST
  - Must wait for writes to complete before continuing
- **Total Store Order (TSO):**
  - Writes can be reordered after reads
  - Write buffers allowed
  - Intel x86 uses this
- **Relaxed models:**
  - ARM, RISC-V: Almost anything can be reordered
  - Need explicit barriers
- **Write in notebook:** Consistency model comparison table

### 📚 DAY 39 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Power Equation Deep Dive

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** Hennessy & Patterson Ch 1.5 pages 25-35 (power and energy)
- **📄 Paper:** "Power: A First-Class Architectural Design Constraint" by Brooks et al. (2000)
- **📄 Paper:** Drepper "What Every Programmer..." Section 6 (pages 70-80) - Power considerations

**Video (0.5 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** "CPU Power Consumption Explained" on YouTube (any hardware channel, 20 min)

**Key Concepts:**
- **Dynamic power:** P_dynamic = α × C × V² × f
  - α: Activity factor (how often transistors switch)
  - C: Capacitance (how much charge to move)
  - V: Voltage (SQUARED! This is huge)
  - f: Frequency
- **Static power:** P_static = I_leak × V
  - Leakage current: Always flows, even when idle
  - Gets worse at smaller nodes (28nm → 7nm)
- **Key insight:** Reduce voltage = QUADRATIC power reduction
  - 10% voltage reduction → 19% power reduction
  - But: Lower voltage = slower transistors = lower max frequency
- **Write in notebook:** Power breakdown pie chart (typical: 70% dynamic, 30% static)

### 📚 DAY 40 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): DVFS Mechanics

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📄 Paper:** "A Comparison of DVFS Techniques" - Survey paper (search Google Scholar)
- **📄 Paper:** "Energy-Efficient Computing" by Barroso & Hölzle (2007)
- **🌐 Website:** ARM DVFS documentation - https://developer.arm.com

**Key Concepts:**
- **Why DVFS works:**
  - P = C × V² × f
  - If reduce f by 20%, can reduce V by ~15%
  - Total power reduction: 0.85² × 0.8 = 58% of original!
- **DVFS operating points:**
  - Turbo: 1.2V, 150 MHz (max performance)
  - Normal: 1.0V, 125 MHz (balanced)
  - Low Power: 0.8V, 100 MHz (efficient)
- **Transition time:**
  - Voltage change: ~10-100 μs (slow)
  - Frequency change: ~1 μs (fast)
  - Always change: freq down → voltage down, voltage up → freq up
- **Write in notebook:** DVFS operating point table with power estimates

### 📚 DAY 41 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Clock Gating Fundamentals

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** "Low Power Design" tutorials at Synopsys website
- **🌐 Website:** https://www.vlsi-expert.com/2011/02/clock-gating.html - Clock gating tutorial
- **📄 Paper:** "Clock Gating Techniques" - any foundry design guide

**Video (0.5 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** "Clock Gating in VLSI" on YouTube (15 min)

**Key Concepts:**
- **What it does:** Turn off clocks to idle modules
- **Why it works:** No clock = no dynamic power
- **Implementation:**
  ```
  assign gated_clk = clk & enable;  // Simple but has glitch!
  
  // Better: Latch-based clock gating
  always @(clk or enable)
    if (!clk) en_latched <= enable;
  assign gated_clk = clk & en_latched;
  ```
- **Where to gate:** Idle cache banks, unused functional units, inactive cores
- **Write in notebook:** Clock gating cell schematic

### 📚 DAY 42 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Power States

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**
- **📖 Read:** ACPI Specification - C-states overview (free PDF)
- **🌐 Website:** Intel C-states documentation
- **📄 Paper:** "Idle Power Management" papers from HotPower workshop

**Key Concepts:**
- **State hierarchy:**
  - Active: Full power, full performance
  - Idle: Clocks on, waiting for request
  - Light Sleep: Clocks gated, fast wake-up (~10 cycles)
  - Deep Sleep: Clocks + some power gated, slow wake-up (~1000 cycles)
  - Off: Power cut, state lost, very slow wake-up
- **Trade-offs:**
  - Deeper sleep = more power savings
  - Deeper sleep = longer wake-up latency
  - If wake too often, sleep costs MORE than staying awake
- **Break-even analysis:**
  - Time_in_sleep × Power_savings > Wake_up_energy
- **Write in notebook:** Power state diagram with transitions

**Reading (1.5 hrs):**

**Reference Tools (0.5 hr):**
- **🌐 Reference:** Micron DDR3 Power Calculator Tool (free online)

**Key Concepts:**
- **DDR3 power modes:**
  - Active: Row open, ready for column access
  - Precharge Standby: All rows closed, low power
  - Power Down (PDE): Clock stopped, ~80% power reduction
  - Self Refresh: Data retained, controller can sleep
- **Power-down policies:**
  - PDE entry: How long to wait before entering?
  - Too aggressive: Latency penalty on wake-up
  - Too conservative: Wasted power
- **Write in notebook:** DDR3 power state diagram with IDD values

### 📚 DAY 46 MORNING THEORY (7:00-9:30 AM): Sparsity in Neural Networks

**Reading (1 hr):**
- **📖 Read:** Hennessy & Patterson Ch 7.8 "Domain-Specific Architectures" - sparsity section
- **📄 Paper:** "Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks" - Han et al., NeurIPS 2015

**Video (1 hr):**
- **🎥 Watch:** "Deep Compression and EIE" - Song Han Stanford lecture (45 min)

**Key Concepts:**
- **The sparsity opportunity:**
  - Modern neural nets: 50-90% of weights are zero (after pruning)
  - ReLU activation: 50% of activations are zero
  - Dense hardware wastes 50-90% of computation!
- **Types of sparsity:**
  - Weight sparsity: Fixed after training, predictable
  - Activation sparsity: Dynamic, changes per input
  - Structured vs. Unstructured sparsity
- **The memory angle:**
  - Zeros don't need to be loaded from memory
  - Compress storage: Only store non-zeros
  - But: Irregular access patterns!
- **Write in notebook:** Sparsity types comparison table

  - Double-buffered for continuous operation

- **📖 Read:** "Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems" - Saad, Ch 3 (pages 87-120)

- **Dense MV:** y[i] = Σ A[i][j] × x[j] → O(N²) operations
- **Sparse MV:** y[i] = Σ A[i][k] × x[col_idx[k]] → O(nnz) operations
- **Memory access pattern analysis:**
  - A values: Sequential (good)
  - x vector: Random based on col_idx (bad!)
- **Write in notebook:** SpMV algorithm pseudocode

### 🎯 WEEK 8 TENSTORRENT ADDITION: DATAFLOW ARCHITECTURE STUDY

**Why This Matters for Tenstorrent:**
Tenstorrent's Tensix cores are **dataflow engines**, not traditional von Neumann processors. Understanding dataflow architecture is essential.

**Add to Week 8 Theory Blocks (2-3 hours total):**

**Theory:** Dataflow vs Von Neumann
- **📄 Paper:** "Dataflow Architectures" - Dennis & Misunas (foundational)
- **📄 Paper:** "Dataflow Programming Models" - survey paper
- **🎥 Watch:** "Tenstorrent Architecture Overview" - any public talks
- **Concepts to understand:**
  - Static vs dynamic dataflow
  - Token-based execution
  - Firing rules and data dependencies
  - Why dataflow helps with sparsity (conditional execution)

**Add to Notebook:**
```
DATAFLOW vs VON NEUMANN:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Von Neumann: Instruction-driven (fetch-decode-execute)      │
│ Dataflow: Data-driven (execute when inputs available)       │
│                                                             │
│ Tenstorrent's Advantage:                                    │
│ - Skip entire operations when data is zero                  │
│ - Natural handling of irregular/sparse computations         │
│ - Better energy efficiency for AI workloads                 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

## 🔥 JIM KELLER ADVANCED TOPICS: INTEGRATED IN MARCH

### ADVANCED TOPIC 1: Hardware Prefetching (Week 9-10)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PREFETCHING: Fetch data BEFORE it's needed                                  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ TYPES TO IMPLEMENT:                                                         │
│                                                                             │
│ 1. SEQUENTIAL (NEXT-LINE) PREFETCHER                                        │
│    - On access to line N, prefetch line N+1                                │
│    - Simple but effective for sequential access                            │
│    - RTL: Add prefetch request on cache miss                               │
│                                                                             │
│ 2. STRIDE PREFETCHER                                                        │
│    - Detect patterns: addr, addr+128, addr+256...                          │
│    - Predict next address in sequence                                       │
│    - RTL: Track last N addresses, detect stride                            │
│                                                                             │
│ 3. STREAM PREFETCHER (ADVANCED)                                             │
│    - Track multiple independent streams                                     │
│    - Each stream has its own stride                                        │
│    - RTL: Stream table with LRU replacement                                │
│                                                                             │
│ METRICS:                                                                    │
│    - Coverage: % of misses eliminated by prefetch                          │
│    - Accuracy: % of prefetches that were actually used                     │
│    - Timeliness: Did prefetched data arrive before needed?                 │
│                                                                             │
│ TARGET: 30% miss reduction with 80%+ accuracy                              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ADVANCED TOPIC 2: Victim Cache (Week 10)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ VICTIM CACHE: Small fully-associative cache for evicted lines              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ WHY INTEL USES THEM:                                                        │
│ - Direct-mapped caches have conflict misses                                │
│ - 2 addresses that map to same index thrash                                │
│ - Victim cache holds recently evicted lines                                │
│ - Conflict miss becomes victim cache hit (1 cycle vs 50+ cycles)           │
│                                                                             │
│ IMPLEMENTATION:                                                             │
│ - Small: 4-16 entries (fully associative)                                  │
│ - On L1 eviction: Line goes to victim cache                                │
│ - On L1 miss: Check victim cache BEFORE going to L2                        │
│ - Swap: If victim hit, swap with L1 evicted line                           │
│                                                                             │
│ RTL STRUCTURE:                                                              │
│ ┌─────────────────┐                                                         │
│ │   L1 Cache      │──miss──►┌─────────────┐                                │
│ │ (direct-mapped) │◄──hit───│ Victim Cache│──miss──► L2                    │
│ │                 │──evict─►│ (4 entries) │                                │
│ └─────────────────┘         └─────────────┘                                │
│                                                                             │
│ EXPECTED BENEFIT: 10-15% reduction in L2 accesses                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ADVANCED TOPIC 3: CXL/Gen-Z Preview (Week 12 Evening Theory)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ CXL: COMPUTE EXPRESS LINK - The Future of Memory Interconnect              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ WHAT IS CXL?                                                                │
│ - Industry standard for CPU-to-device memory coherence                     │
│ - Built on PCIe 5.0/6.0 physical layer                                     │
│ - Enables memory expansion beyond DIMM slots                               │
│ - Allows accelerators to share CPU memory coherently                       │
│                                                                             │
│ THREE PROTOCOLS:                                                            │
│ 1. CXL.io: Standard PCIe I/O (like GPU today)                              │
│ 2. CXL.cache: Device caches host memory (coherent accelerator)             │
│ 3. CXL.mem: Host accesses device memory (memory expansion)                 │
│                                                                             │
│ WHY IT MATTERS FOR YOUR CAREER:                                             │
│ - Every major CPU vendor is implementing CXL (Intel, AMD, ARM)             │
│ - Memory pooling in data centers is the future                             │
│ - Heterogeneous computing requires coherent interconnects                  │
│ - You'll likely work on CXL in industry                                    │
│                                                                             │
│ PAPERS TO READ:                                                             │
│ - "Compute Express Link 2.0" - CXL Consortium Spec                         │
│ - "CXL Memory Tiering" - Intel whitepaper                                  │
│ - "Demystifying CXL" - ACM Computing Surveys                               │
│                                                                             │
│ EVENING READING: Week 12, Days 86-87                                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ADVANCED TOPIC 4: Transactional Memory (Week 11 Evening Theory)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TRANSACTIONAL MEMORY: Future of Parallel Programming                       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ THE PROBLEM WITH LOCKS:                                                     │
│ - Coarse-grained locks: Poor parallelism                                   │
│ - Fine-grained locks: Deadlock risk, complex                               │
│ - Lock-free: Expert-level difficulty                                       │
│                                                                             │
│ TRANSACTIONAL MEMORY SOLUTION:                                              │
│ - Programmer writes: atomic { critical_section }                           │
│ - Hardware tracks reads/writes (read-set, write-set)                       │
│ - If conflict: Abort and retry transaction                                 │
│ - If no conflict: Commit atomically                                        │
│                                                                             │
│ HARDWARE SUPPORT (Intel TSX):                                               │
│ - XBEGIN: Start transaction, track accesses                                │
│ - XEND: Try to commit                                                       │
│ - XABORT: Explicit abort                                                    │
│ - Cache-based conflict detection (uses coherence!)                         │
│                                                                             │
│ CONNECTION TO YOUR WORK:                                                    │
│ - Your MESI coherence is foundation for HTM                                │
│ - Conflict detection uses invalidation messages                            │
│ - Cache as speculative buffer for uncommitted writes                       │
│                                                                             │
│ PAPERS TO READ:                                                             │
│ - "Transactional Memory" - Herlihy & Moss, ISCA 1993 (original)            │
│ - "LogTM" - Wisconsin, HPCA 2006 (practical implementation)                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ADVANCED TOPIC 5: Memory Testing & BIST (Week 9-10)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MEMORY TESTING: Built-In Self-Test (BIST) & March Algorithms               │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ WHY MEMORY TESTING MATTERS:                                                 │
│ - DRAM has defects (stuck-at, coupling faults, retention failures)         │
│ - Must test at production AND runtime                                       │
│ - Memory is the #1 source of system failures                               │
│                                                                             │
│ FAULT MODELS:                                                               │
│ 1. Stuck-At Faults (SAF): Cell always reads 0 or 1                         │
│ 2. Transition Faults (TF): Cell can't transition 0→1 or 1→0                │
│ 3. Coupling Faults (CF): Writing cell A affects cell B                     │
│ 4. Address Decoder Faults (AF): Wrong cell accessed                        │
│ 5. Retention Faults: Cell loses data before refresh                        │
│                                                                             │
│ MARCH ALGORITHMS (Industry Standard):                                       │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ March C- Algorithm (covers SAF, AF, CF):                                │ │
│ │ ⇑(w0); ⇑(r0,w1); ⇑(r1,w0); ⇓(r0,w1); ⇓(r1,w0); ⇑(r0)                   │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ Notation:                                                               │ │
│ │ ⇑ = ascending address order                                            │ │
│ │ ⇓ = descending address order                                           │ │
│ │ w0/w1 = write 0/1                                                       │ │
│ │ r0/r1 = read and expect 0/1                                             │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ Complexity: O(14n) for n memory cells                                   │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                             │
│ BIST IMPLEMENTATION:                                                        │
│ - Hardware test pattern generator (LFSR or counter)                        │
│ - Hardware response analyzer (comparator + signature)                      │
│ - Run at power-on or periodically                                          │
│ - Repair: Activate spare rows/columns for failed cells                     │
│                                                                             │
│ RTL TO BUILD:                                                               │
│ - memory_bist.v: March C- implementation                                   │
│ - bist_controller.v: FSM for test sequencing                               │
│ - fault_logger.v: Record failing addresses                                 │
│                                                                             │
│ PAPERS TO READ:                                                             │
│ - "Testing Semiconductor Memories" - van de Goor (classic textbook)        │
│ - "March Tests for Word-Oriented Memories" - Hamdioui et al.               │
│                                                                             │
│ BUILD IN: Week 9, Day 62-63 (integrate with DDR3 testing)                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ADVANCED TOPIC 6: Error Correction Codes (ECC) (Week 10)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ECC: Protecting Memory from Bit Errors                                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ WHY ECC:                                                                    │
│ - Cosmic rays flip bits (soft errors)                                      │
│ - DRAM cells fail over time (hard errors)                                  │
│ - Data centers REQUIRE ECC (99.999% uptime)                                │
│                                                                             │
│ ECC TYPES:                                                                  │
│                                                                             │
│ 1. SECDED (Single Error Correct, Double Error Detect)                      │
│    - Hamming code + overall parity                                         │
│    - 64 data bits + 8 ECC bits = 72-bit word                               │
│    - Can correct 1-bit error, detect 2-bit error                           │
│    - INDUSTRY STANDARD for DDR4/DDR5 ECC DIMMs                             │
│                                                                             │
│ 2. Chipkill (Advanced)                                                      │
│    - Survives entire DRAM chip failure                                     │
│    - Uses symbol-based Reed-Solomon codes                                  │
│    - Required for enterprise servers                                       │
│                                                                             │
│ SECDED IMPLEMENTATION:                                                      │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ ENCODING (on write):                                                    │ │
│ │ - Calculate 8 parity bits from 64 data bits                             │ │
│ │ - P0 = XOR of bits at positions with bit 0 set in binary               │ │
│ │ - P1 = XOR of bits at positions with bit 1 set in binary               │ │
│ │ - ... (Hamming matrix multiplication)                                   │ │
│ │                                                                         │ │
│ │ DECODING (on read):                                                     │ │
│ │ - Recalculate parity from received 72 bits                              │ │
│ │ - Syndrome = calculated XOR stored parity                               │ │
│ │ - Syndrome = 0: No error                                                │ │
│ │ - Syndrome ≠ 0: Syndrome points to error bit position                   │ │
│ │ - Flip the erroneous bit to correct                                     │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                             │
│ RTL TO BUILD:                                                               │
│ - ecc_encoder.v: 64-bit → 72-bit encoding                                  │
│ - ecc_decoder.v: 72-bit → 64-bit with correction                           │
│ - ecc_scrubber.v: Background read-correct-write for hard errors            │
│                                                                             │
│ INTEGRATION:                                                                │
│ - Add ECC to your DDR3 data path                                           │
│ - Log corrected errors (for monitoring)                                    │
│ - Trigger interrupt on uncorrectable error                                 │
│                                                                             │
│ PAPERS TO READ:                                                             │
│ - "Error Correcting Codes" - Peterson & Weldon (classic)                   │
│ - "Chipkill Correct" - IBM Journal                                         │
│                                                                             │
│ BUILD IN: Week 10, Day 68-69                                                │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### ADVANCED TOPIC 7: Memory Power Optimization Deep Dive (Week 11)
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ MEMORY POWER: The Dominant Power Consumer                                   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                             │
│ WHY MEMORY POWER MATTERS:                                                   │
│ - Memory = 30-50% of system power in servers                               │
│ - Mobile devices: Memory = battery life                                    │
│ - Data centers: Memory power = $millions/year                              │
│                                                                             │
│ DRAM POWER BREAKDOWN:                                                       │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ Component          │ % of DRAM Power │ Optimization                     │ │
│ ├────────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤ │
│ │ Activate (row open)│ 35-40%          │ Row buffer locality              │ │
│ │ Read/Write         │ 25-30%          │ Burst transfers                  │ │
│ │ Refresh            │ 15-20%          │ Selective refresh (RAIDR)        │ │
│ │ Background (idle)  │ 10-15%          │ Power-down modes                 │ │
│ │ I/O termination    │ 5-10%           │ ODT optimization                 │ │
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                             │
│ OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES:                                                    │
│                                                                             │
│ 1. ROW BUFFER MANAGEMENT                                                    │
│    - Open-page policy: Keep row open for hits (good for locality)          │
│    - Closed-page policy: Close immediately (good for random)               │
│    - Adaptive: Switch based on workload                                    │
│    - POWER IMPACT: 25% reduction with smart policy                         │
│                                                                             │
│ 2. POWER-DOWN MODES                                                         │
│    - Active standby: Fast wake-up, 50% power                               │
│    - Precharge power-down: Medium wake-up, 30% power                       │
│    - Self-refresh: Slow wake-up, 5% power                                  │
│    - CONTROLLER MUST: Track idle time, choose mode                         │
│                                                                             │
│ 3. REFRESH OPTIMIZATION                                                     │
│    - RAIDR: Skip refresh for cells with long retention                     │
│    - DSARP: Distributed refresh to reduce peak power                       │
│    - Temperature-aware: Refresh more when hot                              │
│                                                                             │
│ 4. VOLTAGE/FREQUENCY SCALING                                                │

│                                                                             │
